Recent evidence complicates the assumption that multi-agent decomposition is beneficial by default: compute-normalized comparisons report that single agents match or exceed multi-agent systems at equal reasoning budgets, and failure analyses attribute a large share of multi-agent breakdowns to specification and inter-agent verification rather than to component capability. This paper takes that evidence as its starting point and asks a narrower question: which architectural properties, as opposed to which agent topology, determine whether an enterprise agentic workflow is governable, recoverable, and auditable. We formalize an enterprise agentic workflow as a policy-constrained stateful system over agents, tools, workflow state, authorization policies, and human decision points, and establish four elementary results. First, policy soundness is a property of complete mediation of external actions and is independent of agent policy quality, which implies that it survives prompt injection and model failure whereas prompt-level guardrails do not. Second, recoverability and auditability require a durable external projection of every state component on which a consequential decision depends; context-resident state admits observationally indistinguishable histories with divergent correct continuations. Third, under an explicit independence idealization, sequential decomposition into n bounded agents without inter-stage verification bounds end-to-end success by p n , so the value of decomposition is conditioned on handoff verification rather than on specialization, which is consistent with reported empiric…
